paper_metadata.title: Pricing Multiasset Derivatives by Variational Quantum Algorithms

summary: The paper proposes a variational quantum algorithm for pricing multiasset derivatives by solving the discretized Black–Scholes PDE with VQS and estimating the price via a SWAP test. It reports noiseless simulations for a single-asset double knock-out barrier option, with 4-qubit and 6-qubit cases, and states a theoretical complexity of O(1/epsilon^2 (log(1/epsilon))^d) versus classical FDM scaling of O((1/epsilon)^{O(d)}).

experiments.description: Variational quantum simulation (VQS) for pricing a single-asset double knock-out barrier option, with the derivative price obtained from the inner product between the VQS-evolved BSPDE solution and the asset-price probability distribution via a SWAP test.

algorithm.variant: variational quantum simulation for linear ODE/PDE solving applied to the Black–Scholes PDE
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient layered ansatz with repeated RY layers and CZ entanglement layers
algorithm.optimizer: Euler method for classical time integration of variational parameters; L-BFGS-B used only for initial-state fitting in a separate demonstration

hyperparameters.ansatz_structure: m repeated layers of n RY gates followed by CZ entanglement layers
hyperparameters.initial_state_fidelity_result: |1 - alpha0^-2 |<Vbar(0)|nu(theta0)>|^2| <= 1.2e-5 for the payoff-state fitting demo

algorithm.parameter_initialization: VQS parameters initialized so that the ansatz is identity at tau=0 (all zeros); for the separate initial-state fitting demo, L-BFGS-B is used to optimize theta0

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Asset-price grid values and derivative values are encoded in amplitudes of n-qubit registers with Ngr = 2^(nd) grid points; the probability distribution state |p(tter)> and the derivative-price state |Vbar(tter)> are overlapped using a SWAP test
problem_formulation.objective_function: Solve the discretized Black–Scholes PDE with boundary conditions and compute V(0,s0) ≈ e^{-r tter} <p(tter)|V(tter)>
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Boundary conditions are incorporated into the ODE via boundary vector C(tau); knock-out barriers set boundary values to zero

problem_instance.description: Single-asset double knock-out barrier option under the Black–Scholes model

dataset_specification.description: Analytical Black–Scholes dynamics; no market dataset used

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize asset price interval [l,u] into ngr grids; no data preprocessing beyond model discretization
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical simulation comparing VQS-derived prices against the analytical solution and classical FDM; also a separate fidelity maximization demo for initial-state preparation

hardware.framework: NumPy for state simulation; quantum-circuit simulation performed on a simulator

implementation_details.classical_solver: Euler method for VQS parameter evolution; SciPy L-BFGS-B for the initial-state fitting demo; NumPy for simulation
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Analytical probability density p(t,s) used to prepare |p(tter)> in the numerical study; grid discretization of the BSPDE
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Take square root of SWAP-test overlap and discount by e^{-r tter} to estimate the present price

speedup_claims.factor: O(1/epsilon^2 (log(1/epsilon))^d) overall quantum complexity vs O((1/epsilon)^{O(d)}) classical FDM
speedup_claims.conditions: under the stated assumptions for state preparation, VQS, and SWAP-test overlap estimation
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper notes the heuristic nature of variational quantum computation and that the overall complexity is not guaranteed; the claimed advantage is asymptotic and depends on efficient state preparation and bounded normalization factors.

speedup_claims.conditions: when function values on (1/epsilon)^{O(d)} grid points are encoded into O(d log(1/epsilon)) qubits
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a resource-scaling claim, not an empirical benchmark.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/epsilon^2 (log(1/epsilon))^d) for the overall method under stated assumptions; VQS circuit resources are O(poly(d log(1/epsilon)))
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical FDM requires O((1/epsilon)^{O(d)}) time and space

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; only small illustrative simulations at 4 and 6 qubits are reported.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: O(poly(d log(1/epsilon))) circuit resources under stated assumptions; SWAP-test measurements scale as O(1/epsilon^2 (log(1/epsilon))^d).
limiting_factors: No quantum hardware execution is reported
State preparation for |p(tter)> and |Vbar(0)> is assumed rather than demonstrated on hardware
SWAP-test measurement cost still scales exponentially in d through (log(1/epsilon))^d
The paper explicitly notes heuristic variational behavior and no guarantee of overall complexity
Classical FDM baseline is only compared analytically/theoretically, not beaten in an empirical benchmark

notes: The paper does not name a specific QPU or cloud provider; the numerical experiments are described as simulations using NumPy, so hardware.type is simulator_statevector by paper context.
The paper reports the ansatz depth as m layers and gives examples with m=4 and 6 qubits; it does not report a transpiled depth or gate counts beyond asymptotic decompositions.
The SWAP test measurement count is given asymptotically; no concrete shot count is reported.
The paper claims a theoretical asymptotic improvement over classical FDM, but the reported results are only noiseless numerical simulations on 4- and 6-qubit instances.
No practical quantum advantage is demonstrated against a classical implementation on the same problem size.
